questions.question: A 0/0 limit has a square root difference in the numerator. What algebra trick should I try?
questions.expected_answer: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the square-root expression.
questions.evidence_quote: we should try multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the expression involving the square root

questions.question: Why can the sum law not be used for the limit of 1/x + 5/(x(x−5)) as x goes to 0?
questions.expected_answer: Neither term has a limit at 0, so the sum law does not apply; add the fractions first (limit is −1/5).
questions.evidence_quote: Since neither of the two functions has a limit at zero, we cannot apply the sum law for limits

questions.question: Can the limit laws be used for the left-hand limit of the square root of (x − 3) at x = 3?
questions.expected_answer: No. The function is not defined to the left of 3, so the left-hand limit does not exist.
questions.evidence_quote: Since this function is not defined to the left of 3, we cannot apply the limit laws

questions.expected_answer: Over their entire domains.

questions.question: If f is continuous on [0, 2] and f(0) > 0 and f(2) > 0, does the Intermediate Value Theorem prove f has no zero there?
questions.expected_answer: No. The IVT only guarantees values between f(0) and f(2); it cannot rule out other values, e.g. (x − 1)^2 has a zero at 1.
questions.evidence_quote: The Intermediate Value Theorem only allows us to conclude that we can find a value betweenf (0) and f (2); it doesn’t allow us to conclude that we can’t find other values

questions.question: Why does f(−1) < 0 < f(1) not prove that 1/x has a zero on [−1, 1]?
questions.expected_answer: Because 1/x is not continuous on [−1, 1], so the IVT does not apply.
questions.evidence_quote: The function is not continuous over [−1, 1]. The Intermediate Value Theorem does not apply here.

questions.question: If a function is differentiable at a point, is it continuous there?
questions.expected_answer: Yes. Differentiability at a implies continuity at a.
questions.evidence_quote: If f (x) is differentiable at a, then f is continuous at a.
